n: With the wall finished and the doors hung, Nehemiah organizes the people who will guard and serve. Gatekeepers, singers, and Levites take their posts.

f.g: Gatekeepers.

n: He puts two trustworthy men in charge of the city, including his brother Hanani. Hananiah is chosen because he was faithful and reverenced God more than most.

f.g: Commander of the citadel, the fortress beside the temple (Nehemiah 2:8).
Revered God more than most men.

n: Practical security rules: keep the gates closed until well into the morning, lock them while guards are present, and post residents as watchmen, each near his own home.

f.g: Until mid-morning, when everyone is awake and alert.

n: Jerusalem was spacious, but few people lived there and many houses were still in ruins. A wall alone does not make a city — it needs people. This sets up Nehemiah 11.
God inspires Nehemiah to register the people by family. He finds the old list of the first returnees from about ninety years earlier, which he copies next.

f.w: my God put into mine heart

n: The list that follows (verses 6–73) is nearly identical to Ezra 2. It records those who returned from Babylon to their family towns.
Twelve leaders are named here (Ezra 2:2 lists eleven), perhaps symbolizing the twelve tribes. This Nehemiah and Mordecai are different men from the governor and from Esther’s cousin.

f.g: The high priest of the first return, also called Joshua (Haggai 1:1).

n: The lay families begin. Parosh was the largest clan. Small differences in numbers between this list and Ezra 2 likely come from copying errors over time or from different stages of the count.
Shephatiah’s descendants, 372 — the same number given in Ezra 2.
The family of Arah. Here the number is noticeably lower than in Ezra’s list (775).
Pahath-moab’s large clan included two branches, descended from Jeshua and Joab.

f.g: Means “governor of Moab,” perhaps recalling an ancestor’s office.

n: The family of Elam, a name shared with a land east of Babylon.
Zattu’s descendants are counted. Ezra’s list gives 945, a hundred more — an easy mix-up for scribes copying numbers.
Zaccai’s family, 760, the same as in Ezra.

f.g: Related to the name Zacchaeus (Luke 19:2), meaning “pure.”

n: Binnui’s family; Ezra 2:10 calls him Bani.

f.g: Called Bani in Ezra 2:10.

n: The family of Bebai, some of whose members later came with Ezra (Ezra 8:11).
Azgad’s family appears here with over two thousand — far more than Ezra 2:12 gives (1,222). One list may record a later stage.

f.g: Means “Gad (fortune) is strong.”

n: Descendants of Adonikam, whose name means “my Lord has risen.”

f.g: Means “my Lord has arisen.”

n: Bigvai’s large family — a Persian-sounding name, showing how exiles adopted names from their surroundings.

f.g: A Persian name; a different Bigvai was governor of Judah later in the Persian period.

n: The family of Adin, with notably more here than in Ezra’s list (454).
Ater’s family, traced through a line called Hezekiah.

f.g: The family of Ater through his descendant Hezekiah.

n: The family of Hashum, which later had members among those with foreign wives (Ezra 10:33).
Bezai’s descendants, 324.
The family of Hariph; Ezra 2:18 lists the same number under the name Jorah.

f.g: Called Jorah in Ezra 2:18.

n: Here the list shifts from family names to hometowns. Gibeon was an old town just north of Jerusalem.

f.g: Called Gibbar in Ezra 2:20.

n: Men of Bethlehem — David’s hometown and the future birthplace of Jesus — and nearby Netophah return to their roots.
Men of Anathoth, the priestly town where Jeremiah was born. Jeremiah had bought a field there as a sign that Israel would one day return (Jeremiah 32:6-15).
Men of Beth-azmaveth, a village near Jerusalem.

f.g: Called simply Azmaveth in Ezra 2:24.

n: Men of Kirjath-jearim, where the ark of the covenant once rested for twenty years, and two neighboring towns.
Men of Ramah and Geba, towns in Benjamin’s territory north of Jerusalem.
Men of Michmas, site of Jonathan’s bold victory over the Philistines.
Men of Bethel and Ai — Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder to heaven, and Ai, which Joshua conquered.
Men of “the other Nebo,” a town in Judah, distinguished from Mount Nebo in Moab.

f.g: A Judean town, not the mountain where Moses died (Deuteronomy 34:1).

n: “The other Elam” — a second group by that name, with exactly the same count as the first (verse 12).
Harim’s descendants, 320 — a lay family, distinct from the priestly Harim in verse 42.
Men of Jericho, the first city Israel conquered under Joshua, which was later rebuilt.
Men of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, towns in the western lowlands. Ono was where Nehemiah’s enemies tried to lure him (Nehemiah 6:2).

f.g: Later called Lydda (Acts 9:32), modern Lod in Israel.

n: Senaah is the largest group listed — perhaps not a town but a name for poorer or lower-ranked people. Ezra 2:35 gives 3,630.

f.g: Its meaning is uncertain; some think it refers to a class of poorer citizens.

n: Now the priests. Jedaiah’s family belonged to the house of Jeshua the high priest.
Immer’s family, one of David’s twenty-four priestly divisions.
Pashur’s priestly family, 1,247.
Harim’s priestly family. Together the priests numbered over 4,000 — about a tenth of the whole company.
Only 74 Levites returned, far fewer than priests. This shortage explains why Ezra later had to recruit Levites (Ezra 8:15).
Temple singers descended from Asaph, one of David’s chief musicians, whose name appears on several psalms. Ezra 2:41 gives 128.
Six families of gatekeepers, who guarded the temple doors.

f.g: Gatekeepers.

n: The list of temple servants begins. These “given ones” helped the Levites with the heavier temple labor.

f.g: From Hebrew “given” — servants given to the temple.

n: More families of temple servants. Their names, many of non-Israelite origin, suggest some descended from foreigners who joined Israel’s worship.

f.g: Possibly means “bent” or “crooked” — some of these names may be nicknames.

n: Three more families of temple servants.

f.g: Means “white” or “moon.”

n: The list continues with Hanan, Giddel, and Gahar.

f.g: Means “gracious.”

n: Rezin shares a name with an earlier king of Syria, another sign of foreign roots among the temple servants.
Three more families who served the temple.

f.g: Means “strength.”

n: “Meunim” may refer to descendants of the Meunites, a people captured in King Uzziah’s day and later attached to temple service.
Bakbuk means “bottle” — names like these may have been colorful family nicknames.

f.g: Means “flask” or “bottle.”

n: The servant families of Bazlith, Mehida, and Harsha.

f.g: Called Bazluth in Ezra 2:52.

n: One family bears the name Sisera — the same as the Canaanite general defeated by Deborah — another sign of foreign ancestry.
The list of temple servants ends with Neziah and Hatipha.

f.g: Possibly means “seized” or “captive.”

n: Now the descendants of Solomon’s servants — probably families first put to forced labor by Solomon, who later served the temple.

f.g: Means “scribe” or “scribal office.”

n: More of Solomon’s servants’ families.

f.g: Mentioned only in these two lists of returnees.

n: The last of these families. “Pochereth of Zebaim” may mean “gazelle keeper,” an occupation turned family name.

f.g: Probably “keeper of the gazelles.”

n: The temple servants and Solomon’s servants together total 392 — the same total as in Ezra 2:58.
Some returnees came from Babylonian towns but could not prove they were Israelites. Lost records had real consequences.

f.g: “Salt mound” — a settlement in Babylonia.
Prove their family line.

n: These three families, 642 people, were among those who could not prove their ancestry. They still came, wanting to belong to God’s people.

f.g: A family name here, not Nehemiah’s enemy.

n: Some priests also lacked records. One family took the name of Barzillai, the loyal friend of King David, after marrying into his family.
Without written proof of descent from Aaron, these men could not serve as priests. Records mattered because priesthood in ancient Israel was inherited by lineage.

f.g: Ritually disqualified, not morally guilty.

n: The governor ruled that they must not eat the holiest offerings until a priest could inquire of God with the Urim and Thummim. Latter-day Saints recognize this sacred instrument from the Restoration.

f.g: A Persian title for governor, meaning roughly “his excellency.”

n: The total congregation was 42,360, the same total as Ezra 2:64. The family numbers listed add up to fewer, so the total likely includes people not named in the groups above.

f.w: forty and two thousand three hundred and threescore

n: Besides them were over 7,000 servants and 245 singers. The singers here may have been singers for celebrations and mourning, separate from the temple choir.
The returnees brought hundreds of horses and mules for the long journey.

f.g: Valued as sturdy pack and riding animals.

n: Camels and thousands of donkeys carried families and goods across the desert route.

f.g: Donkeys — the common beast of burden.

n: Leaders gave generously toward the work, starting with the governor himself. Nehemiah’s version records the gifts in more detail than Ezra 2.

f.g: Darics — Persian gold coins.

n: Family heads gave large amounts of gold and silver to the building fund.

f.g: Hebrew “mina,” a weight of about 1.25 pounds (0.6 kg).

n: The rest of the people gave too. Everyone, leaders and common folk, offered what they could.

f.w: the rest of the people gave

n: The families settled in their towns. Then, “when the seventh month came” — the sacred autumn month of feasts — the stage is set for the great gathering where Ezra reads the law (Nehemiah 8).

f.g: Tishri, roughly September–October, the month of the Feast of Trumpets, Day of Atonement, and Feast of Tabernacles.
